clues.title: Road line: Dashed yellow lines
text: Yellow dashed lines like this are super common in Ireland. You can find sometimes similar lines in New Zealand so if you are not sure use other clues like landscape/vegetation etc.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines
text: It is very common to see yellow outside dashes on Irish roads.
**NOTE:** This is essentially never found in the UK. These dashes can also be seen in New Zealand.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Burren National Park
text: The area in and around Burren National Park is characterised by a unique karst landscape consisting of exposed grey limestone rocks.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Wicklow Mountains
text: One noteworthy area in the east is the Wicklow Mountains, just south of Dublin. They can look deceptively similar to the western coastal mountains. It can be very hard, if not downright impossible to distinguish these two areas.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Western Mountains
text: Ireland’s west coast is defined by a rugged, hilly landscape. Steep hills and low mountains dominate. The neat fields of the east make way for wild grass- and moorlands. The grass often has more brownish and yellow tones to it. Sometimes you will be able to see exposed rocks.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Tabletop Mountains
text: In the north of counties Sligo and Leitrim you can find distinctive tabletop mountains.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Google car: Donegal
text: If a very small rural road has Generation 4 coverage and is located in an unusually hilly landscape, you are likely to be in Donegal. Note that this meta only applies to the smallest roads: thin, without road lines, and sometimes with grass in the middle. This type of coverage is also not exclusive to Donegal, it is just likely to be there.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Plate: EU Plates
text: Ireland has long, white licence plates with the standard European blue strip on the left.
The white backplate is especially useful to distinguish it from the UK, which uses yellow backplates (but white fronts).
In addition, most UK vehicles lack the blue strip on the left.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Yellow Dashed Outlines
text: It is very common to see yellow outside dashes on Irish roads.
This is essentially never found in the UK.
These dashes can also be seen in New Zealand.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Warning sign: Diamond Warning Signs
text: Ireland is the only European country that uses yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.
This only applies to warning signs.
Regulatory signs (circles and upside down triangles) have the normal red border and white background, like most other European countries.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Chevron: Chevrons
text: Irish chevrons are yellow on black.
Both single and multiple arrows are common.
UK chevrons are white on black.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Pole Warning Signs
text: The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between Ireland and the UK.
The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.
The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped.
They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Give way sign: Yield
text: Irish yield signs feature the word “YIELD”.
UK yield signs have the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Rounded Metal Gates
text: Rural metal gates with rounded corners are very common in Ireland.
This is mainly useful to distinguish it from the UK, where similar gates typically have square corners.
However, gates in Northern Ireland also typically have rounded corners.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Strip Of Grass
text: You will often see a strip of grass in the middle of tiny rural roads.
Such roads are called “boreens”.
While not unique, these boreens can often be a strong clue in a tough 50-50 between Ireland and the UK.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Black Roofs
text: You will usually find cream white buildings with black roofs in Ireland.
Sometimes, the buildings feature grey corner stones.
In cities, you will typically find row buildings.
British style brick buildings can still be found in Ireland.--

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: These green and white bollards can be a good clue for Ireland.
They are not entirely unique to the country, but they are especially helpful in 50-50s with the UK.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: slanted top
text: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: Ireland has a slanted top.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: A & B-Type w/o reflectors
text: Ireland uses (just like Germany) A & B-Type guardrails without any reflectors.
NOTE: The UK only uses A-Type guardrails.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Street sign: Dublin street sign
text: Dublin has blue street signs with white text and a white border around it, it also has a number on the right, showing in which district your in. Here is a map of postal areas in Dublin for guessing within the city.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Cork vibes
text: Cork is relatively unique in that it is significantly more hilly than the other big Irish cities.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Irish
text: Irish is a Celtic language native to the island of Ireland and co-official with English in the Republic of Ireland. Irish signage is often bilingual, with English in a regular font, and Irish in italics. Place names, regular words and phrases are all translated. Irish language is somewhat less common on non-official signage.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
